Hey there, I'm putting together a backyard barbecue for about 20 friends and family this summer and could use some menu ideas that work for both the adults and the kids.

Oh, twenty heads is a lovely size for a gathering! Big enough to feel like a proper party, but small enough that you won’t burn out before the first burger hits the grill. I’ve hosted plenty of backyard shindigs, and the secret to keeping everyone happy—from the picky toddler to the foodie aunt—is keeping things simple, handheld, and a bit messy in a fun way.

Here’s a lineup that usually gets a round of applause at my place.

For the main event, I always do a "build-your-own" burger and hot dog station. It sounds basic, but it works magic. I’ll prep a couple of burgers with standard beef, but I’ll also throw in a few veggie or black bean patties for those who don’t do meat, and maybe some chicken sausages. The key is the toppings. Lay out bowls of everything: lettuce, tomato, onion, pickles, cheese, ketchup, mustard, relish, maybe some jalapeños for the brave ones. Kids love making their own "masterpieces," and adults appreciate having exactly what they want without you running back and forth.

Now, for the sides, you want stuff that doesn’t wilt in the heat. A big bowl of cold potato salad is a staple, but I like to mix it up with a creamy coleslaw too. Something crunchy and cool cuts through the richness of the grilled meats perfectly. I also always make a huge platter of corn on the cob. You can just throw it on the grill with some butter and salt, and it’s universally loved. Kids think it’s like candy sticks, and adults love the smoky flavor.

Don’t forget the dips! A bowl of thick ranch dressing and a bowl of BBQ sauce are non-negotiable. You can serve them with raw veggies like cucumber slices and carrot sticks for a bit of freshness, or just as extra sauce for the burgers. I once forgot the ranch at a BBQ and people were genuinely sad—it’s that important!

For desserts, skip the complicated cakes. Just get a few tubs of vanilla ice cream and some fresh berries or chocolate syrup. Let everyone scoop their own into waffle cones or bowls. It’s easy, it’s cool on a hot day, and it feels special without costing a fortune.

And honestly? Hydration is huge. Have a big cooler with water, maybe some lemonade or iced tea, and a separate one for sodas and beers. Label them clearly so people don’t mix up the kids' juice with the adult drinks.

The vibe is what really sells it, though. Play some good music, keep the grill area organized so you’re not flailing around, and just enjoy the chaos. You’ve got this!
That's a great starting point—how much food should I plan on per person if I'm serving a couple of mains and a few sides?

Right, right, the math bit. I always get a bit nervous about this too, especially with a mixed crowd like that. You don't want to be scraping the bottom of the tub, but you also don't want to be eating leftover coleslaw for a week.

For the mains, if you’re doing burgers and dogs, I usually plan for about two burgers per adult. Some folks are hungry, some aren't, but two is a safe bet. For the kids, one burger or maybe just a hot dog is usually plenty. So, for twenty people, let’s say ten adults and ten kids (roughly), you’d want about twenty burgers and maybe ten to fifteen hot dogs. Honestly, I’d just buy twenty burgers and twenty hot dogs. If there are leftovers, they make amazing breakfast sandwiches the next morning. I learned that the hard way after a wedding where we had forty unserved sausages.

For the sides, volume can be tricky because things shrink when they’re mixed. For potato salad or coleslaw, aim for about a cup per person. That’s roughly two pounds of salad total. It sounds like a lot, but you’ll be surprised how fast it goes when it’s served warm or at room temp. For corn on the cob, I’d say one ear per person is standard, but if you know your crowd loves corn, go for two. Corn is cheap and cheerful, so no harm in having a few extras.

Buns and wraps are the silent killers of a barbecue. I always buy more buns than I think I need. People get hungry, or they want a second helping of condiments. For twenty people, I’d grab three packs of burger buns and two packs of hot dog buns. Better to have a few extra buns sitting on the table than to run out when someone’s hand is reaching for a burger.

Don’t forget the condiments and napkins. It sounds silly, but you’ll need way more napkins than you think. Grilling is messy. I usually grab a big box of paper towels and a few rolls of paper napkins. And for drinks, a good rule of thumb is two drinks per person for the first two hours, then you’ll see how the night goes. But have plenty of ice. Always, always have plenty of ice.

Just keep it loose. If people are happy, they won’t mind if the potato salad runs out slightly early. They’ll just eat more burger.

Hey there, I'm putting together a summer backyard barbecue for about 20 friends and family, and I need some menu ideas that'll keep both the adults and the little ones happy.

Oh, twenty people is a lovely crowd size! Big enough to feel like a proper party, small enough that you won’t have to run around like a headless chicken trying to keep the food warm. I’ve hosted a few of these over the years, and honestly, the secret to keeping everyone happy—from the picky toddlers to the hungry uncles—is going with things that are easy to eat with one hand and don’t require much fuss.

For the mains, I’m a huge fan of the "build-your-own" vibe. You can’t go wrong with a classic burger and dog station. Keep the meat simple: maybe half beef patties, half turkey or chicken burgers for the lighter eaters, and some good old-fashioned hot dogs. The trick is to lay out all the fixings in pretty bowls—lettuce, tomato, onion, pickles, cheese, ketchup, mustard, relish. Let the adults get fancy with their condos and let the kids just slap on some ketchup. It saves you from having to cook twenty different orders, and everyone feels like they’re getting exactly what they want.

If you want to mix it up a bit, tacos are brilliant for this too. Set up a bar with seasoned ground beef, some shredded chicken, black beans for the vegetarians, and then all the toppings: salsa, guacamole, sour cream, cheese, cilantro. Kids love dipping their chips in the salsa and guac, and the adults can get messy with their soft shells. It’s colorful, fun, and keeps the cooking contained to one or two big pans.

Now, for the sides, you want things that are forgiving. A big bowl of potato salad or pasta salad is always a winner. I usually make a creamy potato salad with plenty of hard-boiled eggs and dill; it tastes better the day before anyway, so you can prep it ahead of time. Coleslaw is another must-have—it cuts through the richness of the burgers and dogs. And don’t forget some simple roasted veggie skewers or just plain corn on the cob. Corn is magic for kids; they love holding it and eating it like a lollipop.

For the little ones specifically, I always put out a "kid’s table" with some plain cheese sticks, apple slices, and maybe some mini muffins or soft pretzels. It gives them something familiar to grab if they’re shy about the main food, and it keeps them from raiding the dessert platter before the adults have had a chance.

Drinks are easy: plenty of ice-cold lemonade (kids love that stuff), iced tea, and maybe a pitcher of something fruity for the adults if you’re feeling fancy. Water is a must, especially if it’s hot.

The whole point is to keep it relaxed. If you set up a couple of tables with all the food laid out buffet-style, people can help themselves, and you can actually hang out with your friends instead of hovering over the grill. You’re going to do great—just trust your gut and keep it simple. Enjoy the sunshine and the company!
That sounds like a solid start — any suggestions for how much meat and how many side dishes I should plan per person so I don't run short?

Right, getting the quantities right is the bit that usually keeps people up at night, but it’s actually pretty straightforward once you know the rough rules of thumb. I’ve had a few times where I’ve cooked way too much and ended up eating leftovers for a week, so I’ve learned to keep it tight but with a little buffer.

For the meat, if you’re doing burgers and hot dogs as your main two options, plan for about one burger and half a hot dog per person on average. So for twenty people, that’d be roughly twenty burger patties and ten hot dogs. But here’s the trick: always buy a few extra. Maybe grab twenty-five patties and fifteen dogs. It’s cheaper to have a couple of extra patties sitting in the fridge than to have hungry guests staring at an empty plate. If you’re using ground beef, a pound usually makes four decent-sized patties, so you’d need about five pounds of beef. For the dogs, they usually come in packs of ten, so two packs should cover you nicely with a bit left over.

If you’re leaning towards the taco idea, plan for about a pound of meat per four to six people, depending on how big eaters your crowd is. For twenty folks, three to four pounds of meat (mixed between beef, chicken, and beans) is usually plenty. People tend to fill up on the sides and tortillas more than they do on the meat itself.

Now for the sides, this is where it gets a bit more generous. You want enough so people can have seconds without asking. For potato salad or pasta salad, aim for about a quarter to a third of a pound per person. So for twenty people, that’s five to seven pounds of salad. That sounds like a lot, but it disappears fast, especially with kids digging in. For coleslaw, you don’t need as much—maybe two to three pounds total for the whole group. It’s strong-flavored, so a little goes a long way.

Don’t forget the buns and tortillas! For burgers, one bun per person is standard, but I’d buy a couple of extra packs just in case. Buns can get squished or dropped, and you don’t want to be scrambling for replacements. For tacos, plan for two to three tortillas per person. Kids might only eat one, but the adults often load up on two or three.

And here’s a little secret from my own backyard disasters: ice. You always need more ice than you think. For twenty people, I’d grab at least five to ten pounds of ice, depending on how hot it is. You’ll need it for drinks, for keeping raw meat cold before you cook it, and for any last-minute cooling needs. It’s one of those things you never regret having too much of.

Finally, keep an eye on the crowd as they arrive. If you see people going back for seconds quickly, you might want to pop another batch of patties on the grill early. It’s better to have the food ready and warm than to have people waiting around with empty plates. You’re going to nail this—just keep a relaxed vibe, and everyone will be too busy enjoying the food to notice if there’s a slight shortage or surplus. Enjoy the barbecue!

Hi there! I'm putting together a summer backyard barbecue for about 25 friends and family, and I'd love some menu ideas that work well for both kids and adults.

Oh, that sounds like an absolute treat! Twenty-five folks is a lovely crowd—big enough to have a proper celebration but small enough that you can actually mingle and keep an eye on things. I remember throwing a bash for my whole extended family a few years back, we had about that many people, and I nearly lost my mind trying to keep the kids fed while trying to chat with my aunt. The trick, I found, is keeping the main stuff simple and letting the sides do the talking.

For the main event, you can’t go wrong with a slow-cooker pulled pork or chicken. It’s forgiving if you’re busy greeting people, and it goes on just about anything. I’d suggest making a mild BBQ sauce for the kids and having a jar of spicy hot sauce or a tangier vinegar-based sauce on the side for the adults who like a bit of a kick. Serve it up with a pile of soft white buns, maybe some coleslaw (the creamy kind usually wins with the little ones), and a big bowl of baked beans. If you want to mix it up, a "build-your-own" taco bar is brilliant. You just need seasoned ground beef or turkey, warm tortillas, and bowls of shredded cheese, lettuce, tomatoes, and salsa. Kids love assembling their own little meals, and it keeps them out of your hair for a bit while they focus on their creations.

Now, for the sides, you want things that hold up well in the heat. A simple potato salad with a little celery and onion is always a hit, and macaroni and cheese is practically mandatory for the kids. I always make a big batch of corn on the cob, slathered in butter. It’s cheap, easy to eat with your hands, and everyone loves it. If you want something fresh to cut through all that richness, a big bowl of watermelon chunks with a sprinkle of mint is refreshing and sweet enough to double as a dessert for the younger kids.

Speaking of sweets, save yourself the stress of baking individual cakes. Just put out a couple of large bowls of ice cream with a few classic toppings like chocolate syrup, sprinkles, and maybe some crushed cookies. It’s interactive and feels special without the fuss. And don’t forget the drinks—have a big pitcher of lemonade and plenty of iced tea. I always keep a cooler stocked with water bottles because, let’s be honest, people forget to drink when they’re having fun, and you want to keep everyone hydrated, especially the little ones running around in the sun.

The key is to prep as much as you can the night before. Chop your veggies, mix your salads, and even cook your meat if it’s something like pulled pork that tastes better the next day. That way, on the day of the barbecue, you’re just warming things up and enjoying your own party instead of being stuck in the kitchen. Have a wonderful time, and don’t stress too much—people are there for you and the company, not just the food!
That sounds great — could you also give me a rough estimate on quantities for the main dishes and sides so I don't run short?

Right you are, planning the amounts is the tricky bit. You don’t want to be scraping the bottom of the pot, but you don’t want a mountain of leftovers either. For twenty-five people, a good rule of thumb is to plan for about one pound of meat per adult, but since you’ve got kids in the mix, they’ll eat less meat and more of the sides, so you can scale that back a bit.

For the pulled pork or chicken, I’d aim for about 15 to 16 pounds of raw meat. That sounds like a lot, but bone-in cuts shrink down significantly when they cook. If you’re doing ground beef for the tacos, 10 to 12 pounds should do you nicely. Kids might go for two or three small tacos, but adults might eat four or five, so that average works out. You’ll want about 50 to 60 buns or tortillas. I always buy a few extra just in case someone drops one or wants a second round.

For the sides, you want enough so people can help themselves twice. For the potato salad or mac and cheese, aim for about 10 to 12 cups total. That’s roughly 2.5 to 3 pounds of potatoes or dry pasta before cooking. Coleslaw is lighter, so about 6 to 8 cups should be plenty. Corn on the cob is easy to guess—plan for one ear per person, so 25 ears. If you’re buying them in the husk, they’re cheap and easy to grill or boil.

Don’t forget the buns and tortillas. Get three or four packages of hamburger buns (usually 8 or 12 per pack) and maybe 30 to 40 soft tortillas. It’s better to have a few extras than to run out.

For the drinks, I’d say one gallon of lemonade and one gallon of iced tea is a safe start. People drink more than you think, especially in the heat. Keep an eye on the cooler and top up as needed.

And for the ice cream, a half-gallon of vanilla and a half-gallon of chocolate is usually enough for 25 people if it’s just a scoop or two with toppings. If you want to be fancy, add a quart of something fun like cookie dough or strawberry.

Remember, you can always order more pizza or burgers from a local spot if you’re running low. It’s a safety net that saves the day more times than I can count. Just keep an eye on the crowd and see how they’re eating. If the kids are going through the mac and cheese like wildfire, you might need to whip up a quick batch of extra bread or chips. But with these numbers, you should be in good shape. Enjoy the party!

You could do some beef burgers, but also throw in some veggie patties or chicken sausages for variety. Kids are usually pretty flexible if the bun is soft and the toppings are familiar, like ketchup and cheese. I always find that having a "build-your-own" station works wonders. You lay out the buns, the meats, and then a tray of toppings—lettuce, tomato, onion, pickles, cheese slices—and let everyone assemble their own. It stops the drama of "I don’t like onions" and lets the kids feel like they’re making their own meal.

For sides, coleslaw is a winner because it’s cool, crunchy, and doesn’t need heating. A big bowl of potato salad or pasta salad is great too, as they can sit out for a bit without going bad (just keep them in the shade!). I used to make a massive batch of baked beans for these things—just toss in a can of baked beans, a bit of brown sugar, and maybe some mustard, let it simmer in a slow cooker or a pot on the side burner, and it’s ready to go when you are. It’s foolproof.

Don’t forget the drinks. For the kids, lemonade is always a hit. You can buy it, but honestly, making fresh lemonade with a bit of mint is so easy and makes you look like a pro. For the adults, have plenty of ice for their drinks, and maybe a big jug of iced tea.

As for dessert, keep it light. A big bowl of ice cream with some chocolate syrup and sprinkles lets the kids go wild, and the adults can just have a scoop without feeling too heavy after all that food.

How are you feeling about grilling? Do you have a big enough grill to handle twenty burgers and dogs at once, or are you thinking about staggering them?
That gives me a good starting point — how much food should I estimate per person if I'm doing a mix of meats and sides?

Right, sorting the quantities is the bit that usually causes the most panic, but don't worry, it’s pretty straightforward once you get the hang of it. For twenty people, you want to aim for enough so nobody leaves hungry, but not so much that it’s going to waste.

For the burgers, I’d reckon with about two patties per adult. Some folks might just have one if they’re filling up on sides, but plenty will go for two, especially if they’re hungry from playing in the garden. For the kids, one patty is usually plenty, maybe a small part of a second if they’re big eaters. So, if you’ve got, say, fifteen adults and five kids, you’re looking at around thirty to thirty-five burger patties. It’s always better to have a few leftovers than to run out, and burgers freeze brilliantly if you don’t use them all.

Hot dogs are a bit different. Kids love them, and they’re quick to throw on the grill. I’d suggest about one or two per person. Maybe ten to fifteen hot dogs in total. They’re great as a backup if the burgers take longer than expected or if someone just wants something simpler.

It’s messy, but that’s half the fun of a BBQ, isn’t it?

If you’re worried about the meat taking too long or looking too "heavy" for the younger crowd, burgers are always a safe bet, but here’s a trick I learned the hard way: make "slider" sized burgers. You can do a mix of beef and maybe a veggie or black bean option just in case there’s a vegetarian in the mix, but keep the veggie ones separate so they don’t get lost in the crowd.

Now, for the sides, you want things that can sit out for a bit without going off or getting cold. A big bowl of potato salad is essential. I make mine with a mayo-based dressing rather than vinegar because it’s creamier and the kids usually prefer it. Just keep it in a large tub in the shade. Coleslaw is another winner—it’s crunchy, cool, and cuts through the richness of the meat. And don’t forget the bread. Even if you have burgers and buns, a basket of warm dinner rolls or garlic bread is always gone first. It’s the great equalizer; everyone eats bread.

For the little ones specifically, you might want to have a few "safe" snacks ready that aren’t part of the main meal. Things like cheese sticks, apple slices, or even just plain crackers. Sometimes kids get overwhelmed by the big meal and just want something familiar and simple to nibble on while they’re running around. I remember my nephew once just ate a bowl of plain pasta for an hour while the rest of us were grilling. No harm done, and he was happy.

Drinks are easy: big jugs of lemonade or iced tea, plenty of water, and maybe a cooler full of soda for the kids. If you’re serving alcohol, keep it separate so it’s easy to manage.

The key is really just not overcomplicating it. You don’t need fancy plating or intricate recipes. You need food that tastes good warm from the grill, food that’s easy to eat with your hands, and enough of it that everyone leaves happy. Trust your gut, keep the grill stocked, and don’t stress if things aren’t perfect. People are there for the company and the sun, not a Michelin-star experience. You’ve got this!

For twenty people, you want to aim for that sweet spot where everyone is full but you aren’t storing food in your garage for a month. Here’s how I break it down, keeping in mind that there are kids and adults mixed in. Kids eat like birds, honestly. They might have a tiny bit of everything, or they might just graze on chips. So, I usually calculate food for about twelve "adult" portions and eight "kid" portions, just to be safe.

But if you follow these rough numbers, you’ll likely be right on track. Better to have a few extra burgers than hungry guests, right? You’ll be fine.

The golden rule? Don’t try to be a five-star chef. Everyone will be too busy talking, laughing, and watching the dogs run around to notice if the potato salad isn’t perfectly garnished. Just keep the food flowing, the drinks cold, and the music playing low in the background. You’ve got this!

Hi there! I'm planning a bathroom reno and need some help choosing tiles—can you walk me through the main material options I should be considering?

Oh, I love a bit of a reno chat! It’s proper exciting, isn’t it? Though I’ll be honest, standing in a tile shop with a million choices can make your head spin. I remember doing my own bathroom a few years back, and I nearly walked out with three different samples just because they all looked lovely in the brochure. But once you get stuck in, it’s actually pretty straightforward.

So, let’s have a look at the big ones.

First up, you’ve got **porcelain**. This is honestly the workhorse of the bunch. It’s incredibly tough, dense, and doesn’t soak up water like a sponge. That’s crucial for a bathroom, obviously. You can get it to look like wood, stone, or concrete, so if you want that high-end look without the high-end price tag or maintenance, this is usually the way to go. I’ve got porcelain in my shower, and after a few years of kids running around and me slipping in and out with wet towels, it still looks brand new. It’s just solid.

Then there’s **ceramic**. It’s a bit softer than porcelain and usually cheaper. It’s great for walls because it doesn’t need to take a beating from heavy foot traffic or furniture dragging across it. For floors, it’s fine if you’re not expecting heavy use, but if you’ve got a busy household, porcelain might save you some headaches down the line. The glaze on ceramic is what gives it the color and pattern, so if that chips, you can see the clay underneath, whereas porcelain goes all the way through.

Now, if you’re feeling a bit more fancy, **natural stone** like marble, travertine, or slate is stunning. There’s nothing quite like the real thing. But—and there’s always a bit of a 'but'—it’s high maintenance. Stone is porous, which means it needs sealing regularly, or else your shampoo and soap will stain it. I had a mate who put marble in his shower, and he ended up spending half his weekends buffing it. It’s a beautiful look, but it’s a commitment.

You might also see **quartzite** or **slate** being pushed hard in shops. Slate is fantastic for floors because it’s naturally slip-resistant and looks really rustic and cool. It’s sturdy too. Quartzite is harder than granite and marble, so it’s tough like porcelain but with that natural stone vibe. Just check the slip rating if you’re putting it in a wet area.

And don’t sleep on **glass mosaics** for accents. They’re brilliant for shower walls because they don’t hold grime in the grout lines like big tiles do, and they catch the light beautifully. I used a little strip of glass tile in my shower niche, and it makes the whole space feel brighter. It’s not something you’d want on the whole floor, mind you, as it can be slippery, but for a splashback or a wall feature, it’s a winner.

When you’re down at the shop, don’t just look at the tiles in isolation. Pick up a few samples and hold them up against your vanities and fixtures. Lighting changes everything. What looks grey in the shop might look blue in your bathroom. Also, think about the grout. Large format tiles mean less grout, which means easier cleaning and a sleeker look. Smaller tiles mean more grout lines, which can look charming but need a bit more elbow grease to keep them white.

It’s yours, so make it feel like home. Do you have a particular style in mind, or are you still tossing ideas around?
That's helpful, thanks. How do ceramic and porcelain actually compare when it comes to water resistance and long-term durability in a steamy bathroom?

Ah, right, that’s the million-dollar question, isn’t it? It’s where a lot of people get tripped up because they sound like they’re made of the same stuff, but there’s a proper difference under the hood.

Let’s talk water first. Porcelain is what we call "vitreous" or nearly so. It’s fired at a much higher temperature and under more pressure than standard ceramic. That makes it incredibly dense. Water just doesn’t stand a chance with it. The absorption rate is tiny—often less than 0.5%. That means if you spill a bucket of water or have a leaky showerhead, the tile itself isn’t going to soak it up and get weak or freeze and crack (if you’re in a colder climate, though I imagine you’re not worried about freezing tiles in a bathroom!).

Standard ceramic is a bit more porous. It’s still glazed, so the surface is waterproof, and for walls, that’s absolutely fine. But if you put standard ceramic on the floor and water gets under it—maybe through a cracked grout line or a bad seal around the bath—that water can get into the tile body. Over time, especially in a steamy bathroom where moisture is everywhere, that trapped water can cause the tile to crack or pop off, or worse, rot the substrate underneath. It’s not an overnight disaster, but it’s a slow leak that catches you out.

It’s also easier to find in large-format slabs if you’re going for that seamless, modern look, though big tiles on a floor can sometimes be trickier to get the right slope for draining.

For a shower floor, you really want to think about two main things: slip resistance and water absorption. You don’t want to end up doing the penguin waddle every time you get in, do you? Natural stone is a gorgeous option if you’re going for that spa-like, organic feel. Slate is fantastic because it’s naturally non-slip; it’s got this little bit of texture to it that gives your feet something to grip. Travertine and limestone are beautiful too, with those warm, earthy tones, but they’re a bit more porous. If you go with stone, you’ll need to seal it properly right after installation and then keep up with that sealing every year or so. It’s a bit of maintenance, but it looks absolutely stunning.

Porcelain is probably the most popular choice for a reason. It’s incredibly dense, which means it barely absorbs any water at all. It’s tough as nails and won’t stain easily. The trick with porcelain is making sure you get a tile with a textured finish or an "anti-slip" rating. Some smooth porcelain tiles can be tricky when they’re wet, so look for ones with a matte finish or a stippled surface. You can get porcelain that looks just like stone, wood, or even concrete now, so you don’t have to sacrifice style for practicality.

Ceramic is similar to porcelain but generally a bit softer and more porous. It’s often cheaper, which is nice if you’re watching the budget, but for a shower floor, I’d usually lean towards porcelain just for the durability and water resistance. If you do choose ceramic, make sure it’s rated for wet areas and has a good slip-resistant surface.

Glass tiles are lovely for walls because they reflect light and make the space feel bigger, but I’d steer clear of them for the floor unless they’re specifically textured. Smooth glass is a slippery when wet situation waiting to happen.

One thing I always tell people is to think about the grout, too. In a shower floor, you’re going to be standing on it, and grout lines can trap soap scum and hair. Larger format tiles mean fewer grout lines, which can make cleaning a bit easier, but you have to be careful with the slope of the floor to ensure the water drains properly. If you go with smaller mosaics, the grout lines actually help with the slip resistance, which is a nice bonus.

Why don’t you grab a few samples of the ones you’re thinking about and take them into the shower with you? Pour a bit of water on them and stand on them in your socks or bare feet. That helps, thanks—what should I know about slip resistance and water absorption ratings when comparing ceramic and porcelain?

Right, let’s dig into the nitty-gritty of those numbers. It’s not just about how it looks, is it? It’s about not ending up on your backside in the morning!

For water absorption, you’re looking for the PEI rating or, more accurately for floors, the moisture absorption rate. Porcelain is fired at much higher temperatures than ceramic, which makes it denser. You want a tile with a water absorption rate of 0.5% or less. That’s what makes it "porcelain" rather than just "ceramic." If it’s above that, it’s technically ceramic, and while it’s fine for walls, it’s a bit risky for a shower floor because it can soak up water, freeze if you live somewhere cold (though less likely in a bathroom, still good to know), and stain more easily. So, if you see a tile marked as having less than 0.5% absorption, that’s your gold standard for durability and hygiene.

For a shower floor, you generally want at least an R10. R9 is okay for a dry bathroom floor, but once that water hits it, it gets slick. R10 is the sweet spot for most residential showers—it’s textured enough to give you grip but doesn’t feel like walking on sandpaper. If you have older family members or kids who run about, you might want to look for R11. Anything higher than that is usually for commercial spaces like pool decks or industrial kitchens, and it can be a bit harsh underfoot and harder to keep clean because the texture traps grime.

Another thing to check is the COF, or Coefficient of Friction. In the US, they often use this. You want a static COF of at least 0.42 for interior wet areas. It’s a bit of a mouthful, but essentially, the higher the number, the more grip you have.

Oh, Sunday dinner is the best, isn’t it? There’s nothing like the smell of roasting chicken to make the house feel proper cozy. I’ve got just the trick for that crispy skin you’re after. It’s not rocket science, but there are a couple of little secrets that make all the difference.

First off, you want to get that chicken completely dry before it even hits the oven. Moisture is the enemy of crispiness. I usually pull the bird out of the fridge an hour before cooking and pat it down really well with paper towels, even inside the cavity. If you’ve got time, leave it uncovered in the fridge overnight—that dries the skin out even more, but don’t worry if you’re short on time, just give it a good dry-down.

Then, here’s my favorite bit: salt it generously. I mean *generously*. Rub that salt all over the outside, under the skin if you can get your fingers in there gently, and even inside. The salt draws out more moisture and seasons the meat right through. I like to use a mix of butter and oil for the coating. Butter gives you that lovely golden color and flavor, but pure butter can burn if the oven’s too hot. So, I mix some softened butter with a splash of olive oil or even duck fat if I’m feeling fancy. Rub that mixture all over the bird.

Don’t forget the aromatics! I always stuff the cavity with half a lemon, a few sprigs of thyme or rosemary, and maybe a clove of garlic squashed flat. It keeps the breast meat moist and perfumes the whole kitchen.

For the cooking, I put the chicken on a rack in a roasting tin so the heat can circulate underneath. Start it off hot—about 200°C (400°F)—for the first 20 minutes to get that skin sizzling and crisping up. Then turn it down to 180°C (350°F) for the rest of the cook time. A good rule of thumb is 20 minutes for every 500g (1lb) plus an extra 20 minutes. But honestly, the best way to tell is to check the leg joint; when you wiggle it, it should move loosely, and the juices should run clear when you pierce the thickest part of the thigh.

One thing I learned the hard way years ago: always let it rest! I used to carve it straight away, and all the lovely juices would run out onto the board. Now I tent it loosely with foil and let it sit for 10 to 15 minutes after taking it out of the oven. It stays so much juicier.

While that’s resting, you can make a quick gravy from the pan juices. Just deglaze the tin with a bit of white wine or stock, scrape up all those lovely browned bits (we call that fond), and whisk in a little cornflour slurry if you need it to thicken.

Enjoy your Sunday feast! It sounds like it’s going to be a lovely time with the family.

Oh, absolutely! You can’t have a proper Sunday roast without some solid sides to soak up all that glorious gravy. I’ve got two favorites that always go down a storm with the family.

First up, you’ve got to do roast potatoes. They’re practically mandatory! The secret is double-cooking them. I boil cubed potatoes (maris piper or king edwards work best because they’re a bit floury) until they’re just tender, then I drain them really well and let them steam dry in the colander for a few minutes. While they’re drying, I get a big splash of oil or beef dripping sizzling in the roasting tin. Then I shake the colander gently to rough up the edges of the potatoes—that creates all those little jagged bits that turn into pure gold in the oven. Toss them in the hot fat, season well with salt and pepper, and roast them alongside the chicken that last bit. They come out fluffy as a cloud on the inside and shatteringly crisp on the outside. I swear by a little bit of rosemary chopped up and tossed in there too.

Hi there! I'm planning a Sunday family dinner and could use a solid roast chicken recipe that'll feed about six people.

Oh, a Sunday roast is the absolute best way to wrap up the week, isn’t it? Nothing beats that smell wafting through the house while everyone’s getting settled for the evening. I’ve been making this same basic method for years—it’s forgiving, it’s delicious, and it never fails to get compliments.

For six people, you’re looking at a bird that’s about 1.5 to 1.7 kilograms (roughly 3.5 lbs). That gives you enough meat without it being a mountain of leftovers. The secret to a proper roast isn’t really a secret at all; it’s all about getting the skin nice and dry so it crisps up beautifully. When I first started cooking, I used to rush the bird straight into the oven, and the skin would always end up rubbery. Now, I always pat it dry with paper towels and leave it uncovered in the fridge for a few hours, or even overnight if I’ve got the time. It makes a world of difference.

Right before you pop it in, get your oven heating up to 200°C (400°F). Take the chicken out of the fridge about half an hour before cooking so it takes the chill off. Stuff the cavity with a big knob of butter, a couple of smashed garlic cloves, and a lemon cut in half—squeeze the juice in first, then toss it in. Pull those skin flaps up gently and rub some more soft butter right under the skin onto the breast meat. It keeps it juicy while the skin gets golden.

Season the outside generously with salt and black pepper, and if you’ve got any fresh herbs like thyme or rosemary, tuck a few sprigs under the skin too. I usually toss a few large potatoes and some carrots into the roasting tray around the chicken. Drizzle them with a bit of oil and season them, too. They’ll soak up all that lovely chicken fat and become the best part of the meal, honestly.

Roast it for about an hour and twenty minutes to an hour and a half. You’ll know it’s done when the juices run clear when you pierce the thigh with a skewer, not pink. The real trick, though, is the rest. Once it’s out of the oven, tent it loosely with foil and let it sit on the counter for at least twenty minutes. If you carve it straight away, all that juice runs out onto the board and the meat goes dry. Letting it rest redistributes those juices so every bite is tender.

While it rests, you can easily make a quick gravy from the pan juices. Just deglaze the tray with a splash of stock or water, scraping up all those browned bits, and simmer it down. It’s simple, honest food that brings everyone together. Enjoy your dinner!

First off, you can’t beat a big bowl of creamy mashed potatoes. I know you’ve got roasted ones, but there’s something about a fluffy mash that just feels like a hug in a bowl. I used to make my mash with just water and butter, but once I started using the hot milk from the pan, my kids went mad for it. It’s cheap, it’s easy, and it soaks up that gravy beautifully.

For the green side, I’d go for something bright to cut through all that rich butter and meat. Green beans are a classic for a reason. Just steam them until they’re tender but still have a bit of a crunch, then toss them with a little butter and lemon zest. The acidity wakes up the palate after a few heavy bites of chicken. If you’ve got broccoli, that’s brilliant too. Roast it in the same tray as the chicken for the last twenty minutes or so—just keep an eye on it so it doesn’t burn. The charred bits are delicious.

And honestly? A simple salad is a lifesaver. Just some crisp lettuce, a few radishes, and a light vinaigrette. It sounds fancy, but it’s just washing up a head of lettuce and mixing oil, vinegar, salt, and pepper. It keeps the meal from feeling too heavy, especially if you’ve got a big pile of Yorkshire puddings or bread on the side.

If you’re feeling like treating yourselves, a bit of apple sauce with the chicken is pure comfort. Not the sweet jar stuff, but just cooked down apples with a tiny pinch of cinnamon. It pairs surprisingly well with the savory herbs in the roast.

Keep it simple, though. The chicken is the star, and the sides are just there to support it. You’ve got this!

The secret to getting that skin nice and shatteringly crisp while keeping the meat tender isn’t fancy spices or expensive gadgets; it’s really just about moisture and heat. You want the skin completely bone-dry before it hits the oven. So, once you’ve pulled the chicken out of the fridge, give it a good rinse and then pat it down with kitchen paper until it feels almost sticky. If there’s any dampness left, it’ll steam instead of roast, and you’ll end up with rubbery skin.

I always stuff the cavity with a whole head of garlic cut in half, a few sprigs of rosemary, and a lemon cut in quarters. It keeps the breast meat moist as it cooks and gives the bird a lovely aromatic flavor without overpowering it. Then, take a big knob of softened butter—salted is fine, or unsalted with a pinch of sea salt—and gently slide it under the skin over the breast meat. It bastes the chicken from the inside out as it melts.

Season the outside generously with salt and pepper, maybe a little paprika for color, and tuck the wing tips behind the back so they don’t burn. I like to truss the legs with a bit of kitchen string just to keep the shape neat, but if you don’t have string, just tuck them under the body. Roast it at 200°C (400°F) for about 20 minutes to get the skin starting to crisp up, then drop the heat to 180°C (350°F) for the rest of the time. A good rule of thumb is about 20 minutes per 500g plus an extra 20 minutes.

When it’s done, the juices should run clear when you pierce the thickest part of the thigh, and the skin should be golden brown and crackling. The most important thing, though, is letting it rest. Tent it loosely with foil and let it sit for 15 to 20 minutes before carving. If you cut into it straight away, all those lovely juices will run out onto the board, and you’ll end up with dry meat. I usually just spoon some of the pan juices over the top when serving. It’s foolproof, and your family will be asking for seconds before you’ve even cleared the table. Enjoy that Sunday feast!

Oh, a Sunday roast is the absolute best way to start the week properly. There’s nothing quite like the smell of roasting chicken and garlic drifting through the house to make everyone feel settled. For six people, you’re looking at a nice big bird—probably around 1.5 to 1.7 kilograms (that’s roughly 3.5 to 4 pounds). If you can get one that’s been free-range or organic, it usually has a bit more flavour and better texture, but honestly, any decent supermarket bird will do the trick if you treat it right.

The secret isn’t really the recipe so much as the technique. You want that skin absolutely shattering crisp and the meat juicy. I always make sure the chicken is completely dry before it goes in the oven. If you’ve just pulled it out of the fridge, pop it on a rack in the fridge uncovered for a few hours if you can, or just pat it down really well with kitchen paper. Moisture is the enemy of crispy skin, see?

Here’s how I do it, and it never fails me. You’ll need a good knob of butter—salted is fine, but I usually use unsalted and add plenty of good sea salt—about 50 grams (2 tablespoons). Mix that with the zest of one lemon, a teaspoon of dried rosemary (fresh is lovely if you’ve got it, but dried works just fine), a teaspoon of thyme, and a good pinch of black pepper. Get your hands in there and rub that mix all over the chicken, but most importantly, get it *under* the skin. Loosen the skin over the breast with your fingers gently and slide the buttery goodness right up against the meat. That keeps the breast from drying out while the skin gets golden.

Toss a couple of whole garlic bulbs (just cut the tops off so you see the cloves) and a couple of lemons (cut in half) into the cavity. It sounds simple, but it steams the inside with all that lovely aromatic goodness.

Now, for the veg. You don’t want a soggy bottom, so pile your potatoes and carrots around the bird, not under it. I usually roast about 800g of waxy potatoes, cut into chunks, and maybe a couple of bunches of carrots. Toss them in a bit of oil, salt, and pepper, and scatter them around the tray. If you’ve got a roasting tin with a rack, put the chicken on the rack so the air circulates underneath too.

Pop it in the oven at 200°C (180°C fan/400°F). Let it roast for about 1 hour and 15 minutes to 1 hour and 30 minutes. You know it’s done when the juices run clear when you pierce the thickest part of the thigh, and the skin is deep golden brown. If the skin is getting too dark too fast, just throw a loose piece of foil over the top for the last twenty minutes.

Once it’s out, this is the crucial bit I used to forget early on: let it rest. Tent it loosely with foil and leave it for at least 15 to 20 minutes before carving. If you cut into it straight away, all those lovely juices run out onto the plate, and you’re left with dry meat. Resting lets the juices redistribute back into the meat.

While it rests, you can make a quick gravy from the pan juices. Just scrape up all those tasty brown bits (the fond) from the bottom of the tin with a splash of white wine or chicken stock, simmer it down for a few minutes, and whisk in a knob of butter at the end for shine.

It’s a proper comforting meal. My mate Dave used to stress over thermometers and all that jazz, but I told him, just trust your eyes and the smell. If the house smells like heaven and the skin is crackling, you’re golden. Enjoy your Sunday, and I bet your family will love it.

Hi there! I'm planning a Sunday family dinner and could use a solid roast chicken recipe that would work well for a group of about six people.

Oh, Sunday roast chicken is the absolute best way to bring everyone together. There’s something about that smell filling the house that just makes people stop and smile. I remember my nan used to make a massive one every week, and we’d all circle the table like it was a treasure hunt for the crispiest bits of skin.

For six people, I’d say you’re looking at a bird that’s about 1.5 to 1.8 kilograms. If you go much bigger, it might be a bit much for some, and if it’s smaller, you’ll be fighting over the drumsticks!

Here’s how I like to do it to keep it juicy and golden. First things first, take the chicken out of the fridge about an hour before you plan to cook it. Cold chicken in a hot oven can cook unevenly, so letting it warm up a bit helps. Pat it dry with kitchen paper—this is the secret to crispy skin. Moisture is the enemy of crispiness, so get it as dry as you can.

Preheat your oven to 200°C (or 180°C if it’s a fan oven). You want it nice and hot. Rub the whole bird with a bit of olive oil or melted butter. I usually mix in some salt, pepper, and maybe a little garlic powder or mixed herbs if I’ve got them. Don’t be shy with the salt; it needs to taste like the sea in a good way.

Stuff the cavity with whatever you’ve got lying around. A lemon cut in half, a few sprigs of rosemary or thyme, and maybe a head of garlic with the top sliced off. It smells heavenly when it steams inside.

Now, here’s a little trick I learned after a few dry birds in my youth. Tie the legs together with a bit of kitchen string. It keeps the shape nice and compact so it cooks evenly. If you don’t have string, just tuck the wing tips behind the shoulders.

Put it in a roasting tin. I like to toss some chopped onions, carrots, and celery in the bottom with a splash of water or stock. The chicken drips into this, and it stops the veggies from burning while giving you the most amazing base for gravy later.

Roast it for about 20 minutes per 500 grams, plus an extra 20 minutes at the end. So for a 1.5kg bird, you’re looking at roughly 1 hour and 20 minutes. Halfway through, give it a good baste with the juices in the tin. Keep an eye on it after the hour mark. You want the skin to be that deep golden brown, not burnt. The juices should run clear when you prick the thickest part of the thigh.

Once it’s done, this is crucial: let it rest. Take it out of the oven and leave it on a warm plate, loosely covered with foil, for at least 15 to 20 minutes. If you carve it straight away, all the lovely juices will run out onto the board, and you’ll end up with dry meat. Trust me on this one.

While it rests, you can skim the fat off the juices in the tin, add a splash of white wine or more stock, and whisk in a bit of flour if you want a thicker gravy. Serve it up with some roast potatoes, green beans, and maybe a big bowl of steamed peas.

It’s simple, but it never fails to get a round of applause. Enjoy your Sunday dinner!
That sounds great, thanks! Could you also recommend a couple of side dishes that would pair nicely with the roast chicken?

Oh, you’re in for a treat! There’s nothing quite like the crunch of a perfectly roasted potato next to that tender chicken. Since you’ve got six of you, you’ll want sides that are easy to make in bulk and taste even better when they’ve had a bit of time to mingle with the flavors.

For the potatoes, I’m a massive fan of the classic roasties. You can’t go wrong with Maris Piper or King Edward potatoes—they’re floury enough to get fluffy on the inside and crispy on the outside. Peel them and cut them into big, chunky pieces, not too small or they’ll dry out. Par-boil them in salted water for about five minutes until they’re just tender but still hold their shape. Drain them well and let them steam dry in the colander for a minute.

Here’s the trick: shake the colander gently to rough up the edges. That creates little nubs that will turn into incredible crispy bits in the oven. Toss them in the roasting tin with the chicken fat and a splash of oil, maybe a sprig of rosemary thrown in there too. Pop them in with the chicken for the last 45 minutes or so, turning them halfway through. They’ll be golden and gorgeous.

For something green and fresh to cut through the richness, I love roasted root vegetables. You can use carrots, parsnips, and maybe some swede if you like a bit of bite. Cut them into batons and toss them with a little olive oil, salt, pepper, and perhaps a teaspoon of honey if you want a hint of sweetness. Roast them in a separate tray alongside the chicken, or if your oven is big enough, under it. They take about the same amount of time as the chicken, so it’s all very convenient.

If you want something a bit lighter, steamed new potatoes with mint butter is a lovely, simple option. Just boil them until tender, drain, and top with a knob of butter softened with chopped fresh mint. It’s bright and fresh and balances the heavy roast perfectly.

And don’t forget the gravy! Once the chicken is resting, put the roasting tin on the stove. Stir up the bits stuck to the bottom with a splash of water or stock to deglaze it. Let it bubble for a minute, then stir in a tablespoon of flour to thicken it. Simmer for a few minutes until it’s smooth and rich. It’s going to taste like heaven.

So, you’ve got your chicken, your crispy potatoes, your roasted veg, and that gravy. It’s a proper Sunday feast. Enjoy every bite!

Hi! I just got a 3-month-old Labrador puppy and I'm completely new to this—could you walk me through what a good daily diet and feeding schedule looks like for her?

Oh, wow! Congratulations on the new addition to the family! A three-month-old Lab is an absolute dream, isn’t it? Just be prepared for a lot of slobber and maybe a few chewed-up socks, but honestly, the joy outweighs the mess ten times over. I remember when I first got my boy, Barnaby, back in the day. I was so worried about getting it right because Labs have such big appetites and it’s easy to put a bit too much on them if you’re not careful. But don’t you worry, we’ll get this sorted out for you.

At three months, she’s right in the middle of that rapid growth phase, so her tummy is growing fast, but it’s still pretty small. That’s why we split the food up. You definitely want to feed her three times a day. It keeps her energy levels steady and stops her from getting too stuffed at any one time, which can be risky for big breeds like Labs because of something called bloat, though that’s more common later on, it’s good to get into good habits now.

For the food itself, stick to a high-quality puppy formula. Look for one that’s specifically labeled for "large breed" puppies. This is important because large breed food has a balanced amount of calcium and phosphorus to help her bones grow strong without growing too fast, which can cause joint issues later. I wouldn’t bother with mixing in home-cooked meals just yet unless you’ve got a vet or a nutritionist guiding you, because it’s really easy to miss key nutrients when you're cooking. Just grab a good kibble from a reputable brand—ones that list real meat as the first ingredient are usually a safe bet.

Here’s a bit of a routine that worked wonders for me with Barnaby. Breakfast around 7 or 8 in the morning. Then a lunchtime feed around 12 or 1. And finally, dinner around 5 or 6 in the evening. Try to keep the times fairly consistent every day; dogs love routine, and it helps with potty training too, because she’ll likely need to go out about 15 to 20 minutes after eating.

Now, about how much to feed. Every bag of food will have a chart on the back, but take that with a pinch of salt. It’s a starting point. You’ve got to watch her body condition. You should be able to feel her ribs easily when you run your hand over her side, but you shouldn’t see them sticking out. If she looks like a little barrel, dial it back slightly. If you can’t feel her ribs at all, bump it up a tiny bit. Since she’s a Lab, she’s going to look at you with those big, sad eyes when you turn her away from the bowl. She’ll act like she’s starving even if she’s full. Don’t fall for it! They are natural beggars.

One more thing—keep the feeding area calm. No big distractions. And make sure she’s got fresh water available at all times, not just during meals. Labs can get dehydrated quickly, especially if they’re playing hard.

It’s a bit of a learning curve, but you’re doing great just by asking. She’s lucky to have you looking out for her health so early on. Just enjoy those puppy moments, and don’t stress if one day she eats a bit less or more. As long as she’s happy, playful, and keeping a steady weight, you’re on the right track.
Thanks for that info! How do I go about picking the right brand of puppy food, and are there any ingredients I should make sure to avoid?

Right, narrowing down that brand can feel a bit like walking into a supermarket aisle with a thousand options and no clue where to start. It’s completely normal to feel a bit overwhelmed by all the marketing talk. I remember standing in the pet aisle with Barnaby’s bag, reading every single label until my eyes crossed. Here is how I usually break it down so it doesn’t feel like a chore.

First off, look for the Association of American Feed Control Officials (AAFCO) statement on the bag. It’ll say something like "formulated to meet the nutritional levels established by the AAFCO Dog Food Nutrient Profiles for Growth." That’s just a fancy way of saying the food has been tested and actually has what a growing puppy needs. If it doesn’t say that, put it back. It’s the bare minimum standard.

When it comes to brands, I’d steer you toward ones that are well-established and have a good track record with large breeds. Brands like Royal Canin, Hills Science Diet, Purina Pro Plan, or Eukanuba are solid choices. They spend a lot on research and feeding trials, which means they know what they’re doing. There are also some great grain-free options or boutique brands like Orijen or Acana, but honestly, unless your pup has a specific allergy, grain isn’t the enemy. Many vets are actually moving away from grain-free diets right now because of some heart health concerns linked to certain ingredients like peas and lentils in high amounts. So, a food with named grains like brown rice or oats is perfectly fine and often easier on the tummy.

As for ingredients to avoid, you don’t need to become a chemist, but there are a few red flags. First, stay away from vague meat by-products. You want to see named meats like "chicken," "beef," or "salmon" as the first ingredient. If it just says "meat meal" or "animal fat," you don’t really know what you’re getting. Also, watch out for artificial colors, flavors, and preservatives like BHA, BHT, or ethoxyquin. Nature provides plenty of preservatives like mixed tocopherols (vitamin E), which are much better for her.

And please, for the love of all things holy, keep grapes, raisins, onions, garlic, and chocolate far away from her. Grapes and raisins can cause kidney failure in dogs, and onions and garlic damage their red blood cells. It’s not just about the kibble; it’s about what she might scavenge from the counter. Labs are notorious for their "trash panda" phase.

One trick I used to do was to call my vet and ask, "What brand do you recommend for a large breed puppy?" Most vets have a preferred list based on what they’ve seen work well in their practice. It saves you the headache of reading fifty different labels.

Also, don’t be afraid to buy a smaller bag first if the big ones are intimidating. You can try a 4-pound bag to see how she likes the taste and how her tummy handles it. If she’s getting gas or soft stools, it might not be the right food for her. Every dog is different, even within the same breed. Barnaby was fine with chicken, but my neighbor’s Lab needed salmon because he was sensitive to chicken. It’s all about trial and error until you find the sweet spot.

You’re doing a fantastic job researching this. It shows you really care. Just take it one step at a time, and don’t be too hard on yourself if you pick a brand that turns out not to be perfect. You can always switch it up gradually. Just mix a little new food with the old food over a week or so to avoid an upset stomach.

Hi there! I just brought home a 3-month-old Labrador puppy named Daisy, and I'm feeling a little overwhelmed about what to feed her — could you help me figure out a good dry kibble brand and how often she should eat each day?

Oh, hello! First off, huge congratulations on bringing Daisy home. A three-month-old Lab is basically a furry vacuum cleaner with legs, isn’t it? I remember when I got my first dog, a chaotic spaniel mix named Buster. I spent the first week just staring at the bag of food like it was a math problem I couldn’t solve. It’s completely normal to feel a bit dizzy with all the choices out there.

Let’s tackle the frequency first because that’s the easy win. At three months old, Daisy’s tummy is still pretty small, but she’s burning energy like a furnace. You’ll want to split her daily food into three meals. So, breakfast, lunch, and dinner. Maybe around 7 or 8 in the morning, midday when you’re back home, and then around 6 or 7 in the evening. This helps keep her blood sugar stable and stops her from getting too hungry and grumpy before bed. Once she hits about six months, you can drop it down to two meals a day, but for now, that third meal is a lifesaver for her digestion.

As for the brand, this is where things can get a bit noisy because there’s so much marketing noise. The golden rule isn’t a specific brand name, but rather looking for the label. You want something that says "puppy" or "all life stages" and has a meat source as the very first ingredient. Labs are prone to joint issues later on, so looking for a formula that includes glucosamine and chondroitin is a brilliant move now. I always steer folks toward brands like Royal Canin Labrador Retriever Puppy, Purina Pro Plan Puppy, or Hill’s Science Diet Puppy. They’re not the cheapest, but they’re made by people who actually study dog nutrition, and they’ve got those joint supplements built in. If you’re on a tighter budget, Purina One or Blue Buffalo Life Protection are solid, reliable choices that won’t break the bank but will still give her the protein she needs to grow big and strong.

One thing that really helped me with Buster was establishing a routine. I’d put the bowl down, give her fifteen minutes to eat, and then take it away if she hadn’t finished. It sounds harsh, but it teaches them that mealtime is now, not later. You’d be surprised how quickly they learn!

Also, since she’s three months old, be careful with treats. They should only make up about 10% of her calories. If you’re training her—which you will be, because Labs are smart but sometimes stubborn—use tiny pieces of her kibble as rewards. That way, you’re not overfeeding her while you’re trying to teach her "sit."

Don’t worry if you mess up a meal or two. Dogs are forgiving creatures. Just keep the water fresh, stick to the three times a day, and watch her weight. You want to be able to feel her ribs easily but not see them sticking out. If she’s getting round like a ball, cut the portion slightly. If she’s looking a bit bony, bump it up a little. You’ve got this, and Daisy is lucky to have someone looking out for her like this.
Thanks, that's really helpful! How much food should I be putting in her bowl at each meal, and should I stick to a strict schedule or is it okay to be a little flexible?

Right then, let’s get into the nitty-gritty of the bowl sizes. This is where it gets a bit tricky because every puppy is different, but we can get a really good estimate. Most high-quality puppy foods have a feeding chart on the back of the bag. That’s your best friend right now. You’ll look for her current weight—and honestly, just weigh her on your bathroom scale if you can. If a three-month-old Lab is around 15 to 18 pounds, you’re probably looking at roughly 1.5 to 2 cups of food *per day*, split into those three meals. So, that’s about half a cup to two-thirds of a cup per sitting.

But here’s the thing: those charts are guidelines, not laws. I remember with Buster, I followed the chart exactly for a week, and he was still begging like he hadn’t eaten in days. Turns out, he was just a big eater. The best way to tell if you’ve got the amount right is the "rib test." Run your hands along her sides. You should be able to feel her ribs easily without pressing hard, but you shouldn’t see them sticking out. If she’s getting a bit soft all over, cut back slightly. If she’s looking a bit sharp, give her a little extra. It’s a bit of a dance at first, but you’ll get the hang of it in no time.

Now, about that schedule. I’d say stick to the times as closely as you can. Puppies thrive on routine. It helps with potty training massively because their bodies learn when to expect food and, consequently, when to need to go out. If you feed her at 8 AM, she’ll likely need to go out within 15 to 20 minutes. If you feed her at random times, her digestive system gets confused, and you’ll end up with more accidents in the house.

That said, being a human means life happens. If you’re an hour late one day, it’s not the end of the world. Just don’t make it a habit. Consistency is key, but perfection isn’t required. If you have to shift dinner by an hour because you’re stuck in traffic or working late, just go with it. The important part is that she knows mealtime is a special event, not just a free-for-all where food is available 24/7. Free-feeding (leaving a bowl out all day) is a big no-no for Labs, though. They will eat until they are sick. Trust me on that one.

So, measure out three portions in the morning, put them in separate containers or bags, and just grab one when it’s time. It saves you from guessing every time and keeps things tidy. You’re doing a great job asking all the right questions. Daisy’s in good hands with you!

Sometimes Stansted or Luton will have cheaper direct flights than Heathrow, even if they’re a bit further out of town for you. Airlines like Ryanair often fly from Stansted or Gatwick to Ciampino, and EasyJet flies from Gatwick, Luton, and sometimes Heathrow to Fiumicino. British Airways and Alitalia (now part of ITA Airways) usually fly from Heathrow to Fiumicino, but they might be pricier this late in the day.

If you’re really struggling to find a direct flight that’s affordable, you might want to consider flying into Ciampino instead of Fiumicino. It’s a smaller airport, but it’s often cheaper and closer to central Rome. There’s a bus service that takes you straight into the city, which is quite handy.

BA sometimes has "last minute" deals on their website, so it’s worth a peek.

There’s a direct bus from Ciampino to the city centre that’s reasonably priced and runs regularly.

Rome is such a lively city, and a quick weekend there can feel like a week of history and pasta. Enjoy every minute of it!

It feels more like a local village than a tourist trap, which I love.

Another good area is **Repubblica** or **Via Nazionale**. It’s a bit more bustling and commercial, but it’s super central. You’re close to the Opera House, and it’s a short walk or a quick bus ride to the Vatican or the Spanish Steps. Because it’s a bit more "everyday" Rome, you might find some decent mid-range hotels or B&Bs there that don’t have the heavy tourist markup.

If you’re willing to stay slightly north, near **Termini Station**, you’ll find a lot of budget-friendly options. It’s not the prettiest part of town, and it can be a bit noisy and chaotic, but it’s the transport hub. You can get anywhere from there. Just make sure you pick a hotel on a quieter side street if you book there, so you aren’t woken up by the early morning train announcements.

Always check the reviews for noise levels, because thin walls are a thing in old Roman buildings!
